# Discussion

## Limitations of the study

Although for the experiment that took place in 2023 different species were used, only limited valve data was available due to an issue of data be overwritten. Therefore its use to assess the functioning of the fish spiral was limited. During the first experiment of 2024 this issue was resolved, though it seemed that the temporal resolution of the valve data was too low to capture the moment the valves opened and closed. The last two experiments had sound valve measurement data for the entire duration of the experiment at an adequate temporal resolution. Another important limitation, typical for any laboratory experiment, involves the controlled conditions that not necessarily mimic real-life conditions. Not only will actual river conditions be different from those in the lab, river conditions are also known to vary strongly in time and space. Since in this study laboratory conditions were fixed, the effect environmental conditions might have had, could not be assessed. Finally, the fish themselves, sedated, operated and transported, are unlikely to show the same behaviour (e.g., movement, intent and motivation) as they would under natural conditions [@noonan2012].

## Insights gained

The cycle duration and phase distribution of exp0 (2023) were completely different from the experiments of 2024. For exp0, cycle duration was twice as long and phase distribution was much more comparable between the lower and upper valve. For the experiments of 2024 (exp1 to exp3) the cycle duration and phase distribution can be considered the same, though this was not apparent from the data because of the too low temporal resolution of the exp1 valve-opening data. In contrast with the experiment of 2023, for the experiments of 2024 the lower valve was closed most of the time, while the upper valve was open most of the time.

Despite operational settings of the FSSG throughout the experiments of 2024 being fixed, **passage efficiency and entrance efficiency varied substantially** as they ranged **from 0.47 to 0.79, and from 0.63 to 0.98, respectively**. It is very difficult to determine the underlying cause behind this difference as these values are not exact but underestimations and local, potentially interfering, conditions might have been present but were only sporadically measured (e.g. water quality). In addition, fish were re-used for the different experiments and their familiarity with the system might have had an effect (though the available results do not indicate any effect). **The length, weight and species did not have any effect on whether fish were able to successfully use the fish spiral, nor did it have an effect on the time it took fish to move up the fish spiral.** Only a limited number of fish went through the FSSG multiple times.

Despite their high variability and likely underestimation, both the entrance and passage efficiency in this study were still relatively high. However, it should be noted that fish were forced into the lower basin with no-where else to go than through the lower valve. Whether the provided attraction flow would be strong enough to direct upstream-migrating riverine fish towards the inlet of the FSSG (i.e., What would be the attraction efficiency?) in a real-life situation, could not be assessed under these fixed laboratory settings and would require field tests on sites that resemble the locations the FSSG is intended for. The FSSG therefore has the potential to aid fish in their migration, but placement and sound operational settings will be key. Though the low amount of water that passes through the FSSG is beneficial for water managers that want to prevent too much water to flow from one side of a sluice or hydropower installation to the other, it is not ideal to attract fish and make them move through the system. Both the unnatural low amount and the discontinuous, interrupted supply of water via the inlet are likely to limit the ability for fish to find the FSSG entrance (i.e., attraction efficiency), enter it (i.e., entrance efficiency) and move successfully through it (i.e., passage efficiency)[@bunt2012].

Fish generally **wait until the valves are completely open before entering and leaving the FSSG,** though for the upper valve a relatively large amount of fish also seem to leave the fish spiral when the valve is opening or closing.
